summary: Belize lies on the eastern coast of Central America and is the only country in the region with English as its official language, with Maya ruins and the world's second-longest barrier reef.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Catholicism expanded from the mid-19th century with the large numbers of Mestizos and Maya who fled from Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula to northern Belize; they were refugees of the Caste War that began in 1847. Jesuit missionaries arrived in 1851 and opened schools, and Catholic schools still play an important role in Belizean education today. In recent years, immigrants from Central American countries such as Guatemala and Honduras have continued to increase the number of Catholics.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: Protestantism arrived during the British colonial period with the British and the Creoles, and in the 18th and 19th centuries the Anglican, Methodist and Baptist churches established congregations and schools in Belize City. From the 20th century, denominations such as the Pentecostals, Seventh-day Adventists and Mennonites grew rapidly, and the overall proportion of Protestants is now close to that of Catholics.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious population has grown in recent decades; in the 2010 census more than 15% of people identified as having no religion, mainly urban young people and groups influenced by secularization. Social and economic change, the spread of education, and alienation from traditional churches are all reasons for the rising proportion.

ranking.name: Other religions
ranking.description: Other religions include Islam, the Baha'i Faith, Hinduism, the Garifuna 'dugu' ancestral-spirit ritual that blends African and Catholic elements, and traditional Maya beliefs. These religious communities are small but reflect Belize's diverse ethnic makeup.

religion.background: Ancient Belize was one of the core regions of Maya civilization, and sites such as Caracol show that a developed Maya religion once existed there. From the 17th century British logwood cutters settled along the coast and brought Protestantism; in 1862 British Honduras formally became a British colony. In the mid-19th century, a large influx of refugees from the Caste War in Yucatán made Catholicism the largest religion. After Belize became independent in 1981, society remained religiously diverse, with Catholic, Protestant and non-religious populations coexisting.

language.official: English is the official language, but Spanish and Belize Kriol are more common in daily life.

ranking.name: Spanish
ranking.description: Spanish speakers increased greatly after the mid-19th century, as the Caste War in Yucatán from 1847 sent large numbers of Mestizos and Maya fleeing to the north. During the Central American civil wars of the 1980s, large numbers of refugees from Guatemala, El Salvador and Honduras moved in as well, making Spanish the mother tongue of the largest number of people, concentrated in the northern and western regions.

ranking.name: Belize Kriol
ranking.description: Belize Kriol formed in the 17th–18th centuries between British logwood cutters and the slaves they brought from Africa and Jamaica; its vocabulary is mainly English, while its grammar is influenced by West African languages. During the colonial period it became the common language of Belize City and the central region, and it remains the most commonly used lingua franca among the different ethnic groups.

ranking.name: Maya languages (Q'eqchi' and others)
ranking.description: The Maya languages include Q'eqchi', Mopan and Yucatec Maya, and their speakers are descendants of the inhabitants of ancient Maya civilization. Most Q'eqchi' and Mopan people migrated from Guatemala to the southern Toledo District between the late 19th century and the 20th century to escape forced labor and land dispossession; they still live by traditional agriculture and have preserved their mother tongues.

ranking.name: English
ranking.description: English is the official language of Belize, originating from British colonial rule from the 17th century onward; from 1862 to 1981 Belize was called British Honduras. English is used in government, the courts and schools, but because Kriol and Spanish are more common in daily life, only about 6% have standard English as their mother tongue.

ranking.name: Low German (Mennonite)
ranking.description: Low German (Plautdietsch) is the language used by Mennonites, descendants of the 16th-century Anabaptists of the Netherlands and Germany who migrated successively to Russia, Canada and Mexico. In 1958 more than three thousand Mennonites moved from Mexico and Canada to Belize, where they established agricultural communities in the west and north, and they still maintain their own language and way of life.

language.history: Belize was the center of Maya civilization in ancient times, and Maya languages have a history of several thousand years there. In the 17th century British logwood cutters settled along the coast, and contact with African slaves produced Belize Kriol; in 1862 British Honduras became a British colony and English became the official language. The Caste War in Yucatán in the mid-19th century and the Central American civil wars of the late 20th century brought large numbers of Spanish-speaking immigrants, and the Garifuna and the Mennonites also brought their own languages. After independence in 1981, Belize became the only country in Central America with English as its official language, while retaining a rich multilingual environment.

ranking.name: Rice and beans
ranking.description: Rice and red kidney beans are stewed together in coconut milk with onion, garlic and thyme, usually served with stewed chicken, potato salad and fried plantain.
ranking.history: Rice and beans comes from the rice-and-beans tradition that West African slaves brought to the Caribbean and Central America, while Belize's addition of coconut milk was influenced by Jamaican and Caribbean culture. During the British colonial period, Creoles ate rice and beans as everyday food in logging camps and cities. Today it is regarded as the national dish of Belize, and the Sunday lunch of 'rice and beans with stew chicken' is a tradition in almost every Belizean household.

ranking.name: Fry jacks
ranking.description: Dough made from flour, baking powder and oil is cut into triangles or squares and deep-fried into puffy, hollow pastries, often served with honey, jam or refried beans.
ranking.history: Fry jacks are the star of the traditional Belizean breakfast, a combination of the flour of the British colonial period and the Caribbean tradition of fried dough. After the flour imported by the British became common in the colony, Creole families used it to make all kinds of fried dough pastries. Today at breakfast stalls in Belize City, fry jacks are often served with scrambled eggs, beans and cheese, the breakfast combination most familiar to locals.
ranking.imageCredit: US Embassy Belize・Public domain・Wikimedia Commons

ranking.name: Hudut
ranking.description: Fish is stewed with coconut milk, spices and vegetables into a thick soup, eaten with mashed plantain; it is richly coconutty and creamy in texture.
ranking.history: Hudut is a traditional dish of the Garifuna, a people of mixed African and Carib indigenous descent formed on the island of Saint Vincent in the 17th century; in 1797 the British exiled them to the island of Roatán off Honduras, after which they settled along the Central American coast, and from 1802 some moved to southern Belize. Every year on November 19 Belize celebrates 'Garifuna Settlement Day', and hudut is an indispensable dish at the festivities; Garifuna language, dance and music were also inscribed as a Masterpiece of the Intangible Heritage of Humanity in 2001.

ranking.name: Tamales
ranking.description: Corn dough is wrapped around chicken or pork and a red chili sauce, wrapped in banana leaves and steamed, giving a soft, tender texture with the fresh fragrance of banana leaf.
ranking.history: Tamales are among the oldest dishes of Central America; the ancient Maya and Aztecs already steamed filled corn dough. In Belize, tamales are often made at Christmas and on important holidays, and wrapping tamales together is an important family activity. They also reflect the influence of Mestizo and Maya culture in northern Belize, and are similar to the versions made in Mexico's Yucatán region.

ranking.name: Salbutes
ranking.description: Small corn tortillas are fried until crisp outside and soft inside, topped with shredded chicken, shredded cabbage, tomato and pickled onion, a one-bite snack.
ranking.history: Salbutes originate from the Maya cuisine of Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, and the name comes from Yucatec Maya, meaning 'light food'. During the Caste War in the mid-19th century, large numbers of Yucatán refugees fled to northern Belize and brought this tortilla snack with them. Today it is one of the most common street snacks in northern Belize and Belize City, often sold together with the similar 'panades'.
